newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian president no obstacle to growth - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Colombian president no obstacle to growth - analyst.

text.p: Foreign investors are eager to see Colombia's scandal-plagued President Ernesto Samper resign, but believe the prospects for stable growth will not be hampered even if he serves out his term, a U.S. market analyst said.

Santiago Millan, a New York-based economist with Caspian Securities, predicted investor confidence would be boosted by a thaw in icy relations between the United States and Colombia as the fight against drug trafficking ceased to be a major domestic issue after the U.S. presidential elections in November.

"Investors would definitely like to see Samper leave to put an end to the allegations that he received drug money...But although Samper will stay in office until 1998, leaving an unsettling element in place, the improvement in relations with the United States will allow for a more stable climate," he said.
Samper has been dogged by accusations that he accepted millions of dollars from the Cali drug cartel to fund the 1994 campaign that landed him the nation's top job.
But he was cleared of any wrongdoing by Colombia's Congress this summer and has shrugged off subsequent calls for his resignation.
Millan highlighted Tuesday's announcement that the United States was to give Colombia increased aid to beef up its drug war as a sign of warmer relations between the two.
During his trip to the United Nations this week, Samper welcomed the U.S. decision.

Back at home he is urging Congress to speed up the passage of a package of stiffer penalties for drug traffickers with an eye on winning back U.S. certification and regaining his U.S. visa, withdrawn in July because of his alleged links to drug kingpins.

Millan added that the latest guerrilla offensive is not unsettling foreign investors. The offensive was unleashed nationwide a month ago, and has so far cost the lives of more than 150 members of the security forces and civilians.
"It's an internal problem and not really destabilizing the government. Investors would be afraid if it was going to affect the rules of investment or economic stability," he said.
